name.verbatim: Introduction

longDescription.verbatim: The transmittal of a bill from a representative's or senator's office to the respective chief clerk's office for acceptance and numbering. Across the Desk The official act of introducing a bill or resolution. The measure is given to the Chief Clerk or his or her representative at the Assembly Desk in the Assembly Chambers or to the Secretary of the Senate or his or her representative in the Senate Chambers. It then receives a number and becomes a public document available from the bill room.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The legislator hands the draft law to the chief clerk. The clerk assigns it a number (like AB 123) and makes it a public document. This step is often called 'putting it across the desk.'

shortDescription.verbatim: The transmittal of a bill from a representative's or senator's office to the respective chief clerk's office for acceptance and numbering.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: A legislator formally submits their proposed law to the clerk, who gives it an official number.

name.verbatim: First Reading

longDescription.verbatim: The initial introduction of a bill. The clerk assigns it a number and reads its title and sends the bill to be printed. The bill is then referred by the Rules Committee to a standing committee for a future hearing.
longDescription.plainLanguage: This is the first formal time the bill is considered by the full chamber. The clerk reads the title, prints the bill, and the Rules Committee decides which policy committee will review it next.

shortDescription.verbatim: The initial introduction of a bill. The clerk assigns it a number and reads its title and sends the bill to be printed. The bill is then referred by the Rules Committee to a standing committee for a future hearing.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The bill's title is read aloud in the chamber. It is then sent to a specific committee for review.

name.verbatim: Hearing

longDescription.verbatim: A committee meeting convened for the purpose of gathering information on a specific subject or considering specific legislative measures. Hearing, Public A formal session of a legislative committee, whereby interested members of the public are invited to present testimony on a proposal; distinguished from an informational briefing, which the public is usually allowed to attend but not present testimony.
longDescription.plainLanguage: Committee members meet to review the bill's details. They hear testimony from supporters, opponents, and experts. The public can attend and speak during these hearings.

shortDescription.verbatim: A committee meeting convened for the purpose of gathering information on a specific subject or considering specific legislative measures.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: A committee meets to discuss the bill and hear from experts and the public.

name.verbatim: Second Reading

longDescription.verbatim: Each bill introduced must be read three times before final passage. This is the first order of business on the Daily File. The House approves or denies committee recommendations at this stage. This is usually accomplished without debate or vote.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The full chamber reviews the bill again. They vote to accept or reject the changes recommended by the committee. This step often happens quickly without much debate.

shortDescription.verbatim: Each bill introduced must be read three times before final passage. This is the first order of business on the Daily File. The House approves or denies committee recommendations at this stage.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The bill is read again, and the chamber votes on whether to accept the committee's changes.

name.verbatim: Third Reading

longDescription.verbatim: Each bill introduced must be read three times before final passage. The stage at which bills are eligible for Floor debate and final vote. Third Reading Analysis A summary of a measure ready for Floor consideration. It contains most recent amendments and information regarding how Members voted on the measure when it was heard in committee.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The bill is read one last time. Legislators debate its merits and cast their final votes for this chamber. If it passes, it moves to the other house.

shortDescription.verbatim: Each bill introduced must be read three times before final passage. The stage at which bills are eligible for Floor debate and final vote.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The final chance for debate and a vote in this chamber before the bill moves to the other house.

name.verbatim: Approved by the Governor

longDescription.verbatim: Approved by the Governor The signature of the Governor on a bill passed by the Legislature. Enactment or Enacted into Law The act of passing legislation involves both Houses of the Legislature. A bill moves through the legislative process and if agreed upon by both houses, is sent to the Governor. If the Governor signs the bill or allows it to become law without his signature, it is enacted into law.
longDescription.plainLanguage: After both houses pass a bill, it goes to the Governor. The Governor has 12 days to sign it, let it become law without signing, or veto (reject) it. If vetoed, the legislature can try to override the veto with a two-thirds vote.

shortDescription.verbatim: The signature of the Governor on a bill passed by the Legislature.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The Governor reviews the bill and decides whether to sign it into law or veto it.

name.verbatim: Chapter

longDescription.verbatim: After a bill has been signed by the Governor, the Secretary of State assigns the bill a 'Chapter Number' such as 'Chapter 123, Statutes of 1998,' which subsequently may be used to refer to the measure. Statutes Compilation of all enacted bills, chaptered by the Secretary of State in the order in which they become law.
longDescription.plainLanguage: Once signed, the bill is compiled into the official state laws called 'Statutes.' It is now enforceable and has a unique chapter number.

shortDescription.verbatim: After a bill has been signed by the Governor, the Secretary of State assigns the bill a 'Chapter Number' such as 'Chapter 123, Statutes of 1998,' which subsequently may be used to refer to the measure.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The bill is officially part of state law. The Secretary of State gives it a chapter number for reference.

name.verbatim: Held in Committee

longDescription.verbatim: Held in Committee The defeat of a measure by the decision of a standing committee not to return it to the full house for further consideration. Dropped Author has decided not to pursue the passage of the bill. Pass on File: When the House refuses to pass and retain a measure on the agenda, it is passed on file. Whenever a bill has been passed on file twice on two successive legislative days on the Third Reading File, it shall be placed on the Inactive File.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The bill did not become law. This can happen if a committee refuses to review it, it fails a vote in the chamber, or the author decides to stop supporting it.

shortDescription.verbatim: The defeat of a measure by the decision of a standing committee not to return it to the full house for further consideration. Dropped Author has decided not to pursue the passage of the bill.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The bill did not become law because it was rejected by a committee, failed a vote, or was withdrawn by its author.

description.verbatim: The California legislative sessions is biennial -- it occurs over a two-year period. Biennium A two-year period. This term is used to describe the two-year term of a Legislature that begins in an odd-numbered year and ends in an even-numbered year.
description.plainLanguage: California's legislature meets for two years at a time. Each session starts in an odd-numbered year and ends in the following even-numbered year.

definition.verbatim: The official act of introducing a bill or resolution. definition.verbatim: A bill passed by the Legislature and approved by the Governor.
definition.plainLanguage: A law that has been passed by both houses of the legislature and signed by the Governor.

definition.verbatim: Disposition of any question before the Legislature.
definition.plainLanguage: Any official decision or step taken by the legislature on a bill or issue.

definition.plainLanguage: The final end of a legislative session. No more meetings will be held for that session.

definition.plainLanguage: A change proposed by a legislator during a full chamber meeting, rather than in a committee.

definition.plainLanguage: A legislature with two separate chambers, like the Assembly and Senate.

definition.plainLanguage: A draft of a new law that a legislator proposes.

definition.verbatim: A brief summary of the purpose, content and effect of a proposed measure or amendment for committee and Floor proceedings.
definition.plainLanguage: A short summary explaining what a bill does and how it affects current law, used by legislators to make decisions.

definition.plainLanguage: The Governor's power to remove specific spending items from a bill without rejecting the entire bill.

definition.verbatim: When the provisions of one chaptered bill amends the same code section as another chaptered bill. Chaptering out can be avoided with the adoption of 'double jointing' amendments. (Absent 'double jointing' language, the code section as amended by the bill with the higher chapter number takes effect and 'chapters out' the code section as amended by the bill with the lower chapter number.)
definition.plainLanguage: When two laws change the same rule, the one passed later (with a higher chapter number) overrides the earlier one.

definition.verbatim: A group of legislators, usually members of the same house, assigned to consider a subject or issue and to submit a report on its recommendations for action by the body which created it. All committees are appointed by the Speaker of the Assembly.
definition.plainLanguage: A smaller group of legislators who review bills in specific areas, like health or education, before they go to the full chamber.

definition.plainLanguage: When the first house agrees to changes made to their bill by the second house.

definition.verbatim: Committee-Conference Committees Appointed from both houses to reach agreement on a measure for final approval by both houses once it has been passed in differing versions by each house.
definition.plainLanguage: A temporary group of legislators from both houses who meet to agree on the final text of a bill when the two houses have passed different versions.

definition.verbatim: Prepared by the Legislative Counsel, it summarizes the effect of the proposed bill on current law. (See Bill Digest and Legislative Counsel's Digest.)
definition.plainLanguage: A summary prepared by legal staff explaining how a proposed bill would change existing laws.

definition.verbatim: An affirmative recommendation made by a committee; moves a bill to the Floor or to the next committee, as specified, without amendment.

definition.verbatim: Double Jointing occurs when two bills amend the same code section but in different ways and the Legislature wants both to happen. Technical amendments are drafted which add provisions to the bill that would make all of the changes in a section of a code, or general law proposed by that bill effective by that bill and one or more other bills, if each bill is chaptered. Double jointing prevents the problem of chaptering out.
definition.plainLanguage: A technique used when two bills change the same law in different ways. It ensures both changes are included in the final law instead of one overriding the other.

definition.verbatim: Whenever a bill is amended, the printed form of the bill is proofread to make sure all amendments are inserted properly. After being proofread, the bill is 'correctly engrossed' and is therefore in proper form.
definition.plainLanguage: After a bill is changed, staff proofread it to make sure every change is correctly typed into the official copy. The cleaned-up version is called engrossed.

definition.verbatim: Whenever a bill passes both Houses of the Legislature, it is ordered enrolled. Upon enrollment, the bill is again proofread for accuracy and then delivered to the Governor. The 'enrolled bill' contains the complete text of the bill with the dates of passage certified by the Chief Clerk of the Assembly and the Secretary of the Senate.
definition.plainLanguage: The final, official version of a bill after both houses have passed it. It is sent to the Governor for signature.

definition.verbatim: When amendments to a bill remove the current contents in their entirety and replace the contents with different provisions.

name.verbatim: Step 1: How Your Idea Becomes A Bill

label.verbatim: contact your legislator to communicate your position on the bill

longDescription.verbatim: The Member then sends the idea and the language for the bill to the Legislative Counsel's Office where it is drafted into the actual bill. The drafted bill is returned to the legislator for his or her review. Persons or groups that originated the idea for the bill may also review it to ensure that the provisions they desire are in the bill in the correct form. If the author is a Senator, the bill is introduced at the Senate Desk; if an Assemblymember, at the Assembly Desk, where it is assigned a number and read for the first time.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The legislator sends their idea to professional staff who write the legal text. Once written, the legislator reviews it. If approved, the bill is officially introduced in the chamber where the author serves, given a number (like AB 123), and read for the first time.

shortDescription.verbatim: All legislation starts off as an idea. these ideas can come from anybody and the process begins when either an individual or group persuades a Member of the Legislature to author a bill.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: A legislator agrees to write and introduce a new bill.

name.verbatim: Step 2: What To Do When Your Bill Goes To Policy Committee

longDescription.verbatim: Since bills are not heard in policy committee until 30 days after they have been introduced and printed, there is plenty of time to investigate a bill or contact your legislator to communicate your position on the bill. Each bill must appear in the Daily File for four days prior to being heard in a committee. The Daily File is the agenda of the day's business, together with public notice of bills set for committee hearings.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The bill is assigned to a specific policy committee (like Education or Health). It must wait 30 days after introduction before a hearing can be scheduled. The committee will decide if the bill should move forward based on its policy merits.

shortDescription.verbatim: The bill then goes to the Senate or Assembly Rules committee where it is assigned to a policy committee.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: A specialized committee reviews the bill's content and impact.

name.verbatim: Step 3: What If Your Bill Goes To A Fiscal Committee?

label.verbatim: prepare your written comments before the committee meets

longDescription.verbatim: At this point, you should inform the members of the committee why you support or oppose the bill based on a fiscal argument. The finance committees are concerned about fiscal impact and not policy considerations. Try to see the staff analysis that has been done on the bill by the policy committee, the Department of Finance, and/or the Legislative Analyst.
longDescription.plainLanguage: If the bill costs money or affects taxes, it goes to the Appropriations Committee. This committee focuses only on the financial details, not the policy ideas. You can argue for or against the bill based on its cost.

shortDescription.verbatim: If the bill has a fiscal impact or a state cost, it will be heard in either the Senate or Assembly Appropriations Committees.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: A committee reviews the bill's financial impact on the state budget.

name.verbatim: Step 4: After Your Bill Passes The House Of Origin And Goes To the Second House

label.verbatim: Communicate to your legislator or the author which amendments you prefer and why

longDescription.verbatim: On Third Reading, the author presents the bill for passage by the entire house. Most bills require a majority vote (it must pass by 21 votes in the Senate and 41 votes in the Assembly), while urgency measures and appropriation bills require a two-thirds vote (27 in the Senate, 54 in the Assembly).
longDescription.plainLanguage: The full Assembly or Senate debates and votes on the bill. A simple majority (41 votes in the Assembly, 21 in the Senate) is usually needed to pass. Urgency measures and budget bills need a two-thirds supermajority.

shortDescription.verbatim: Third Reading is the last stage that a bill goes through in the House of Origin before it passes to the second House to go through the committee process all over again.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: The full chamber votes on whether to send the bill to the other house.

name.verbatim: Preparation and Circulation of Petition

longDescription.verbatim:
A proponent has only 90 days from the date of the enactment of a bill* to request and receive a circulating title and summary from the Attorney General, print petitions, gather the required number of valid signatures, and file the petitions with county elections officials. (Elec. Code, §§ 9006, 9014(c).) It should be noted that the Attorney General has 10 days to prepare the circulating title and summary. (Elec. Code, § 9006(b).)

The petitions must be signed by registered voters in an amount equal to at least 5% of the votes cast for all candidates for Governor at the last gubernatorial election, which was held on November 8, 2022. The total number of valid signatures required to qualify a referendum for the ballot is 546,651. (Cal. Const., art. II, § 9(b).)
longDescription.plainLanguage: Supporters must act quickly: they have just 90 days from when a law is enacted to gather signatures. They first request an official title and summary from the Attorney General, who has 10 days to prepare it. Then, they print petitions and collect signatures from registered voters. To qualify, they need signatures equal to at least 5% of the total votes cast for Governor in the last election. For example, after the 2022 gubernatorial election, this required 546,651 valid signatures.

shortDescription.verbatim: A proponent has only 90 days from the date of the enactment of a bill to request and receive a circulating title and summary from the Attorney General, print petitions, gather the required number of valid signatures, and file the petitions with county elections officials.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: Supporters have 90 days after a law is passed to get an official title, print petition forms, and collect enough valid voter signatures.

name.verbatim: Signature Verification: Random Sample

longDescription.verbatim:
Within 30 business days of the SOS’s random sample notification, county elections officials are required to verify the validity of the signatures filed with their office using a random sampling technique of verification. (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 2, § 20521.) The elections official is required to verify at least 500 signatures or 3% of the number of signatures filed in their county, whichever is greater. Counties receiving fewer than 500 petition signatures are required to verify all signatures filed in their county. (Elec. Code, § 9030(d).) Upon completion of a random sample, the elections official immediately certifies to the SOS the number of valid signatures appearing on the petitions filed in their counties. (Elec. Code, § 9030(e).) The SOS then applies a formula to determine the projected statewide total number of valid signatures. (Elec. Code, § 9030; Cal. Code Regs., tit. 2, §§ 20530-20532, 20540.)

Under 95 Percent:
If the total number of valid signatures is projected to be less than 95% of the number of signatures required to qualify for the ballot, the measure is deemed to have failed to qualify. The SOS must immediately generate a failure notice and mail a copy to the proponent(s) and county elections officials. (Elec. Code, § 9030(f).)

Over 110 Percent:
If the statewide random sample total projects more than 110% of the required number of valid signatures (601,317), one of the following will occur depending on how many days remain before the next statewide general election. (Elec. Code, § 9033(c).)

Between 95 Percent and 110 Percent:
If the statewide random sample total projects between 95% and 110% of the required number of signatures, the SOS notifies county elections officials to verify every signature on the petition. This process is referred to as a “full check.” (Elec. Code, § 9031(a).)
longDescription.plainLanguage: After petitions are filed, county officials verify a random sample of signatures to estimate the total valid count statewide. If the sample shows fewer than 95% of the required signatures, the measure fails immediately. If it shows more than 110%, the measure is projected to qualify. If it falls between 95% and 110%, officials must check every single signature (a 'full check') to be sure.

shortDescription.plainLanguage: County officials check a random sample of signatures to estimate if enough valid ones were collected statewide.

name.verbatim: Qualified for the Ballot

longDescription.verbatim:
If at least 131 days remain before the next statewide general election, the referendum would be eligible, but not yet qualified, for that ballot. On the 131st day before that election, the SOS must issue a certificate certifying that the referendum is qualified for the ballot.

If fewer than 131 days, but not fewer than 31 days, remain before the next statewide general election, the SOS must immediately issue a certificate certifying that the referendum is qualified for that ballot.

If fewer than 31 days remain before the next statewide general election, the referendum would be eligible for the following statewide general election ballot. On the 131st day before that election, the SOS must issue a certificate certifying that the referendum is qualified for the ballot.
longDescription.plainLanguage: The timing of qualification depends on how close the petition filing is to the next election. If filed more than 131 days before the election, it qualifies for that election. If filed between 31 and 131 days before, it qualifies immediately. If filed within 31 days, it moves to the next general election.

shortDescription.verbatim: If at least 131 days remain before the next statewide general election, the referendum would be eligible, but not yet qualified, for that ballot. On the 131st day before that election, the SOS must issue a certificate certifying that the referendum is qualified for the ballot.
shortDescription.plainLanguage: If enough time remains before the election, the Secretary of State issues a certificate officially placing the measure on the ballot.

name.verbatim: Referendum on the Ballot

longDescription.verbatim:
Once on the ballot, voters will be asked whether they want to “Keep the law” or “Overturn the law” (rather than “Yes” or “No” as with all other ballot measures). (Elec. Code, § 13247.)

If voters cast more votes to “Keep the law” than to “Overturn the law,” the statute that is subject to a referendum takes effect on the fifth day after the SOS certifies the election results, unless the statute that is subject to a referendum provides otherwise. (Cal. Const., art. II, § 10(a).)

If voters cast more votes to “Overturn the law” than to “Keep the law”, the statute is repealed.
longDescription.plainLanguage: On election day, you will see 'Keep the law' or 'Overturn the law' instead of 'Yes' or 'No'. If more people vote to keep the law, it stays in effect. If more people vote to overturn it, the law is repealed.
